title: Coil-built wide flared fruit bowl
subtitle: A broad open bowl with a flared rim, built from coils on a pinched base
excerpt: This fruit bowl is built from stacked coils over a pinched base, widening as the coils rise and then flaring outward at the top to create a wide open mouth. The coils are blended smooth inside and out. Made from air-dry clay and sealed inside, the bowl holds fruit but is not a food-safe surface: use a liner for anything moist.
sourceNotes: Coil-building technique derived from first principles. Wide-mouthed bowl form documented across multiple ceramic traditions; construction references derived from traditional hand-building methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rope of clay rolled to even diameter, used as the building unit in coil construction.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to trim and blend.
Clay dissolved in water to a thick paste, used as adhesive when joining clay pieces.
Air-dried but unfired clay. Fragile; the final stage before sealing an air-dry piece.

projectSchedule.title: Build the base and first coils
projectSchedule.body: Pinch the base and stack the first five coils. Cover loosely and leave to stiffen overnight.

projectSchedule.title: Add the upper coils and flared rim
projectSchedule.body: Stack the remaining coils and flare the rim. Blend all surfaces inside and out.

projectSchedule.title: Seal and finish
projectSchedule.body: Sand, paint if desired, and apply three coats of acrylic sealant to the interior.

content.text: A coil-built bowl has a different quality of line from a thrown one. The walls are built up by hand so they carry minor variation in thickness and height: a slight irregularity that makes the bowl look handmade. This version flares outward at the top to create a wide, open mouth. The
coil
structure is blended smooth inside and out so the finished bowl reads as a unified form rather than a layered one.
What you'll need
Around 700 g of air-dry clay for a bowl with a 25 cm mouth diameter and a 10 cm base. A cup of
slurry
(tablespoon of clay dissolved in water).
Building the base

Pinch a thick base disc 10 cm across and 8 mm deep. Press it flat on the work surface and smooth the bottom with the wooden rib to flatten it. The base must be stable: rock it to check; trim any high spot with the fettling knife.

Roll the first coil to 12 mm diameter and long enough to circle the base. Score the top of the base disc and the underside of the coil. Apply slurry to both surfaces and press the coil onto the base rim. Blend the interior joint downward into the base with the wooden rib, pulling the coil clay into the disc to create a strong structural join.
Building upward

Add five more coils, each placed fractionally further out from the previous to create the bowl's outward curve. Score, slurry, and blend the interior join on each coil before moving to the next. The exterior can remain rough at this stage.
After six coils, cover the piece with a damp cloth and leave to stiffen for 30 minutes. The lower section should reach
leather-hard
before the next coils are added. Test by pressing the wall gently: it should hold its shape but still yield slightly.

Once the lower section is stiff, add the flared top. The top three coils each sit slightly inward from the coil below for two coils (to draw the form in slightly), then the final coil sits outward to create the outward flare. This profile: widening, then slightly narrowing, then flaring open: gives the bowl more visual depth than a straight-sided taper would.
Smooth the exterior wall with the wooden rib, working from base to rim in short upward strokes. Blend all coil lines away. Then smooth the interior in the same way.
Smooth the rim with a dampened fingertip, rolling it slightly inward to close the edge and prevent chipping.
Drying

Cover loosely with a plastic bag and leave for 48 hours. A bowl of this size dries slowly through the centre of the walls: the rim and the base dry first. After 48 hours under the bag, remove it and allow to air-dry for another 24 hours. The piece is
bone-dry
when it feels uniformly light and room-temperature against the palm.
Finishing

Sand the exterior with 240-grit sandpaper to remove any remaining surface roughness. Apply three coats of acrylic sealant to the interior. Two coats on the exterior is enough for a piece that will hold dry fruit. The sealed piece holds fruit but is not food-safe for cut or moist food: use a liner plate or paper for anything that will shed juice.
Variations
Build in paper-clay-air-dry for a stronger, lighter bowl that will hold up better to daily movement.
Leave two or three coils visible on the exterior as a decorative band rather than blending them completely smooth.
Crimp the top coil with finger pinches at 2 cm intervals to create a decorative wavy rim.

rows.problem: Form collapses outward as more coils are added
rows.cause: Lower section not allowed to stiffen before continuing; coils too wide in diameter
rows.fix: Wait for the lower half to reach leather-hard before adding upper coils. Reduce coil diameter to 10 mm.

rows.cause: Wooden rib not used on the final pass; surface slightly dry
rows.fix: Dampen the wooden rib lightly and make final smoothing passes with the rib rather than a fingertip for a cleaner surface.

rows.problem: Rim dries unevenly and becomes wavy
rows.cause: Uneven coil thickness around the final ring
rows.fix: Roll the final coil carefully to an even diameter before placing it. If unevenness appears while still leather-hard, use the needle tool to trim a level rim.
